items.title: Former Porn Star Reveals Key to Unlocking Shame, Embracing Freedom
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Shame is not God's intention for your life."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

If anyone knows the grip of shame, it’s a former porn star.

Joshua Broome spent years in the pornography industry before finding faith in God, abandoning a life driven by sexual sin and drug abuse, and becoming a husband and father to four boys.

Since his salvation 11 years ago, Broome has become an outspoken evangelist and advocate against the dangers of pornography. One of the barriers to healing, he explained to CBN News, is shame.

“Shame is not God’s intention for your life,” he said. “The solution to shame is connection, is confession.”

Before he learned the Gospel, Broome said it was shame — rather than enjoyment— that kept him trapped in the pornography industry for years. He explained that, while guilt reveals, “I’ve done something wrong,” shame wrongly convinces a person, “I am someone wrong.”

“If I believe that my only value is indicative of me selling myself for sex, well, then, of course I’m going to continue doing what I’ve done, because it’s just an overflow of who I am,” he said.

From the Old to the New Testament, the Bible is clear about the need for confession for spiritual healing.

In Proverbs 28:13, King Solomon wrote, “People who conceal their sins will not prosper, but if they confess and turn from them, they will receive mercy” (NLT).

Then, in 1 John 1:8-9, it’s written, “If we claim we have no sin, we are only fooling ourselves and not living in the truth. But if we confess our sins to him, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleans us from all wickedness” (NLT).

And in James 5:16, James wrote, “Confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The earnest prayer of a righteous person has great power and produces wonderful results” (NLT).

The key to breaking the cycle of shame, Broome emphasized, is honest and complete confession.

“The depth of your confession is going to equate to the level of your healing,” he said. “So say all of it.”

He continued, “The way that you own your past is you have to own it, and the way that you own it is you say it out loud because we can only be as free as we’re willing to be honest.”

For many, Broome said, the root of pornography use is not lust or even sex; more often than not, it’s tied to something much deeper: insecurity, loneliness, an unhealthy understanding of intimacy.

The truth is conversations about past sins or sin struggles are not easy. Broome and his wife, Hope, have had their fair share of difficult conversations over his sexual history. But the truth is, while accountability and responsibility are essential to spiritual growth, confession should be met with compassion.

“[My wife] looked at me and said, ‘Hey, I don’t want to minimize your pain … but I do want to tell you that you’re not defined by the worst thing you’ve ever done, and you won’t be defined by the greatest thing you ever do, because you’re not the author of you — God is,'” Broome recalled. “At the cross, the worst of us meets the best of God, and He wins. That’s how you defeat shame.”

Broome and his wife are the hosts of a new six-part series from XO Marriage, “Made Whole: Healing, Wholeness, and Holiness in a Sex-Saturated World.” You can access the course for free here.

Watch our wide-ranging conversation with Broome in the video above.

items.title: Celebrity Wishes for Perez Hilton’s Recovery — Then Takes It Back: Why?
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Perez Hilton’s livestream was the stuff of nightmares — a potentially demonic episode — and has laid bare the dark underbelly of social media, in more ways than one.

On the periphery of the scandal, a TikTok live video feed that ran nearly half an hour and showed Hilton covered in blood and repeatedly harming himself, was another troubling indication of cultural decay: a society that cares not about praying for our enemies but about getting even.

Jared Padalecki, who rose to fame in the early 2000s as one of the stars of “Gilmore Girls,” has used his clout to advocate for mental wellness, so it’s particularly striking to see him not only rescind but apologize for wishing Hilton well amidst his recovery from what was and will be a decisively defining and deeply dark moment in his life.

Initially, Padalecki wrote on social media, “I hope you are trying as best as you can to be kind to yourself right now. Please surround yourself with the love and support that all humans deserve.”

It wasn’t long before the “Supernatural” star faced swift condemnation for his kindhearted message to the celebrity gossip blogger. Padalecki deleted the post and apologized for publicly hoping for healing for Hilton, telling critics he “didn’t know” about the columnist’s career.

Padalecki went on to apologize for his “words caus[ing] any harm” and added he hopes everyone is “taking care of yourselves.”

It was Padalecki’s first instinct — his wish for Hilton’s healing — that was correct, regardless of Hilton’s checkered past and his indefensible work as a gossip blogger, actions that undoubtedly caused harm to the celebrities who were subject to his coverage.

That’s exactly what Jesus commands of us as His followers in Matthew 5:44-47 (NLT).

“But I say to you,” Jesus preached, “love your enemies! Pray for those who persecute you! In that way, you will be acting as true children of your Father in heaven.”

He went on to say, “For He gives His sunlight to both the evil and the good, and He sends rain on the just and the unjust alike. If you love only those who love you, what reward is there for that? Even corrupt tax collectors do that much. If you are kind only to your friends, how are you different from anyone else? Even pagans do that.”

Then, in Romans 12:17-21 (NLT), the Apostle Paul warned against taking revenge or seeking vengeance against others:

Never pay back evil with more evil. Do things in such a way that everyone can see you are honorable. Do all that you can to live in peace with everyone. Dear friends, never take revenge. Leave that to the righteous anger of God. For the Scriptures say, ‘I will take revenge; I will pay them back,’ says the Lord.

Instead, ‘If your enemies are hungry, feed them. If they are thirsty, give them something to drink. In doing this, you will heap burning coals of shame on their heads.’

Don’t let evil conquer you, but conquer evil by doing good.

Our petition for God to intervene for the healing of another human being made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) should never be predicated on what he or she has done in the past. Rather, it should be evidence of an outpouring of gratitude for a forgiveness gifted to us by a Savior who asks each of us to forgive one another in the same way God, through Jesus, has forgiven us (Ephesians 4:32).

Hilton, who in recent months has professed a faith in Jesus, needs prayer — regardless of the sins of his past.

All of us should absolutely be held accountable for our errors, missteps, and wrongdoings; taking responsibility for our actions is a necessary consequence of the choices we each make in this life. None of that, though, absolves us of the duty to pray for those around us or to need the prayers of others.

In the King James Version translation of 1 Peter 2:9, the Apostle Peter wrote that believers are “a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people” in the world.

While social media is preying on our worst instincts — our fallen nature — to belittle, disparage, and denigrate, we follow a God who is calling us to do the opposite, to be peculiar by praying for the redemption of those trapped in dark places distant from the Lord.

As the psalmist wrote, I pray that, even as Hilton walks through the “darkest valley,” he would find the Shepherd who “leads me beside peaceful streams,” “renews my strength,” and “guides me along right paths” (Psalm 23:1-4, NLT).

items.title: Plague of Lies
items.author: Monica La Rose
items.summary: “What a cruel act to be untruthful,” German theologian and monk Meister Eckhart once wrote in a poem that contrasts relationships built on trust and honesty with those damaged by lies. He described truthful, loving words as “wonderful spices mixed into the days.” But lies, he
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

“What a cruel act to be untruthful,” German theologian and monk Meister Eckhart once wrote in a poem that contrasts relationships built on trust and honesty with those damaged by lies. He described truthful, loving words as “wonderful spices mixed into the days.” But lies, he emphasized, are like earthquakes in the mind and poison to the soul: “Havoc is created in the mind that can no longer trust someone once loved . . . . a plague is spread by one who cannot tell the truth.”

The imagery of a plague spread by falsehoods might seem stark. But to take speech seriously resonates with how our words and their impact are described throughout Scripture. When Paul describes to new believers the difference between life before and after their union with Jesus, words take center stage. “Do not lie to each other,” the apostle emphasizes, “since you have taken off your old self with its practices and have put on the new self” (Colossians 3:9-10).        

There are many reasons to be tempted to lie or distort the truth. Sometimes we might think it’s the best way to protect ourselves or others. But through Christ’s love, through His Spirit at work in our hearts, we learn a different way—one transformed by “compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience” (3:12). And we learn how forgiveness and love can create the kind of trust and peace that brings rest to our souls (v. 15).

items.title: Wounds That Build and Heal
items.author: Marvin Williams
items.summary: According to research, Gen Z can detect a false compliment from a mile away. While the intention might be kindness, the members of that generation value something deeper: genuine respect and honesty. Not looking to be flattered, they want to be believed in. When truth is spoken, they feel respected,
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

According to research, Gen Z can detect a false compliment from a mile away. While the intention might be kindness, the members of that generation value something deeper: genuine respect and honesty. Not looking to be flattered, they want to be believed in. When truth is spoken, they feel respected, taken seriously, and are challenged to grow. But this is likely true for most of us.

Psalm 141:5 gives voice to this wisdom. David wrote, “Let a righteous man strike me—that is a kindness; let him rebuke me.” In his prayer to God, he asked that he would welcome loving wounds from friends as kindness (v. 2; see also Proverbs 27:6). David was intimating that real love doesn’t dodge difficult conversations. It tells the truth, not to shame people, but to help be drawn to God and not “be drawn to what is evil” (Psalm 141:4). This passage reminded David’s listeners that wise, truthful feedback isn’t about tearing others down but building them up.

Let’s not fear receiving correction from the right sources, and let’s not shy away from offering it either. We don’t need more sugar-coated words. We need people who are willing to speak the truth in love. Sometimes, the words that sting the most are the ones that build us, heal us, and help us become who God made us to be.

items.title: Carlos Whittaker: Stop Cutting Off Everyone You Disagree With
items.author: John Taylor
items.summary: Carlos Whittaker’s closest friendship almost didn’t survive 2020. The two men were tight enough that the friend stood up at Whittaker’s wedding. Then came the election, COVID-19 and a summer of arguments about racism in America. They kept landing on opposite sides, and the friendsh
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Carlos Whittaker’s closest friendship almost didn’t survive 2020.

The two men were tight enough that the friend stood up at Whittaker’s wedding. Then came the election, COVID-19 and a summer of arguments about racism in America. They kept landing on opposite sides, and the friendship went quiet.

What brought it back wasn’t a conversation. It was soccer.

When Nashville got a Major League Soccer team, Whittaker and his friend bought season tickets next to each other.

“Every Saturday, he and I show up, and we root for the same team, and suddenly, we’ve got something to root for together,” Whittaker says. “And guess what? That stupid little season ticket has started to heal things in our relationship that I never thought.”

No debate. No apology. No resolution to whatever they’d been arguing about. They just kept showing up next to each other, and the friendship came back on its own.

It’s a small case study for something Whittaker has been arguing for years now: proximity does work that arguments can’t.

Algorithms serve up people who already share our politics, theology and cultural instincts. Group chats keep close friends close without anyone leaving the house. And when someone does say something irritating enough, there’s an unfollow button waiting. It’s never been easier to build a life where almost everyone agrees with you, and Whittaker thinks people are paying for that convenience without realizing it.

He’s watched the shift happen inside his own family. When he was a teenager, hanging out with friends meant physically going somewhere. His son hasn’t needed to.

“When I was growing up, to hang out with my friends, I had to get in my car and drive to hang out with them,” Whittaker says. “But now, my 16-year-old son still doesn’t even have his driver’s license yet. And he doesn’t care. Why? Because he can get on the Xbox and hang out with his friends. He doesn’t have to leave to be with his friends.”

Technology didn’t invent division. It just made avoiding difference effortless. A person can now build an entire social world without a single meaningful interaction with someone who votes differently, believes differently or sees things from a different vantage point entirely.

Whittaker isn’t asking people to become best friends with everyone who disagrees with them. He wants disagreement to stop functioning as automatic grounds for distance.

“Everybody that disagrees with you is not bad for your mental health,” he says.

He’s careful here. Whittaker has ended relationships to protect his own mental health, and he’s not arguing every relationship deserves to survive regardless of the cost. But he thinks the language of boundaries has become a convenient way to avoid the discomfort of being challenged.

“Far too many people are living in silos and bubbles these days,” he says. “We’re limited in our growth as humans.”

His alternative is a line he repeats whenever someone pushes him to publicly weigh in on whatever’s dominating the news cycle that week.

“I don’t stand on issues. I walk with people.”

Walking with people, for Whittaker, is how a conviction becomes something more than an opinion about a headline.

“For every issue I have an opinion on, I find somebody directly affected by that issue, and I try to walk with them, whether at a coffee or lunch,” he says. “It doesn’t mean I’m becoming best friends with the person, but I’m walking with them.”

An opinion about a category of people is easy. A relationship with an actual person complicates the certainty. Whittaker points to Jesus as the model: be human, see humans, free humans. The middle step is the one modern life makes easiest to skip.

“How do we truly see the people in front of us and around us?” he says. “Everyone wants to be seen. Everyone wants to be valued. Everyone wants to know that they matter.”

Seeing people, in his definition, means moving toward people outside your usual circle on purpose.

“Find somebody that’s not like you and see them truly,” he says. “See them. Be curious about them. Be curious about their lives. Build relationships with people who are different from you, not to change them but to be changed by them.”

Whittaker points to something Barack Obama has warned about: a generation mistaking criticism for activism.

“Criticism does not equal activism,” Whittaker says. “What is the action that follows your conviction? We can be convicted about things, but what’s the action?”

For Whittaker, the action is rarely dramatic. Have coffee. Share a meal. Buy the season tickets. Stay close enough to someone that disagreement doesn’t get the last word.

Every Saturday, he’s still at that soccer game, sitting next to a friend he almost lost, rooting for the same team.

“We may not agree on anything,” he says, “but I can still walk with them.”

items.title: A Deeper Dive into ‘Magnifica Humanitas’ with the Word on Fire Institute
items.author: Dr. Joshua Bitting
items.summary:
Dr. Joshua Bitting

You don’t need to arrive with any expertise, just the willingness to stick with it for six weeks and an open mind to let the pope’s wisdom take root.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Joshua Bitting

The Word on Fire Institute will be embarking on a six-week summit delving deeply into Magnifica Humanitas to explore various topics with accessible teachings, debate, pastoral scenarios drawn from real-life situations, and space to think alongside others asking the same questions. UK Program Director, Brenden Thompson, joined me to discussed more of what we can expect from the summit.

Joshua Bitting: Brenden, thank you for heading up this summit on Magnifica Humanitas, the first encyclical by Pope Leo XIV, which focuses on the dignity and safeguarding of the human person in an era of rapid growth in artificial intelligence. What’s the purpose of this summit, and what are you hoping our audience will gain from it?

Brenden Thompson: During the public reception of Magnifica Humanitas, I was most intrigued by the reaction of the political commentator and podcaster Alastair Campbell, well known as former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair’s spokesman. As someone who once said of the Labour government of the late ’90s and early 2000s that “we don’t do God,” his warm reception of the document indicated to me something of the special quality of this first encyclical of Pope Leo XIV. 

Soon after the encyclical was released, Campbell shared with his The Rest Is Politics podcast audience that on the recommendation of someone involved in the world of AI, he decided he would take a look at Magnifica Humanitas. He was full of praise for the first encyclical he, a non-Catholic skeptic, had ever read and spoke of how he was genuinely moved and provoked by its insights and analysis. 

How marvelous that someone in the world of AI recommended a document from the pope to a non-Catholic who not only read it but spoke about it like someone who had just watched a riveting film in the cinema and could not wait to tell people about it. In short, I want those who take part in this Word on Fire Institute summit to embody both halves of this story: the passion of someone who’s just encountered something remarkable and the instinct to share with others. 

In this encyclical, Pope Leo has given all of us—everyone touched directly or indirectly by AI—a great gift. This summit is a chance to receive that gift. It is an opportunity to take our lead from the Holy Father, to slowly journey through his meditations and to let them reshape how we see technology and, more fundamentally, what it means to be human.

This summit also has a broader aim to avoid the risk that this document gets flattened into a single-issue document. Many already speak of Magnifica Humanitas as simply “the AI encyclical.” AI is of course a central theme of the document, but we want to give people an opportunity to go beyond shallow analysis and offer the slower discernment it deserves. Six weeks is not long enough to cover everything in depth, but we hope it is long enough to inspire a cohort of people who can see and share some of the richness it contains.

Artificial intelligence is a topic that evokes a strong response from many people, and perhaps polarized responses ranging from daily use of it to a determination not to engage with it. We released a course on evangelization and artificial intelligence earlier this year. Clearly, the Word on Fire Institute is determined to engage with new forms of technology and to find how to evangelize in this new world. What do you see as the major opportunities and challenges for Catholics engaging with AI and how it will shape our culture?

In Magnifica Humanitas, Pope Leo invites readers into a space beyond outright suspicion and uncritical acceptance. His invitation is more demanding. It’s an invitation to discover how to engage deeply with this topic so that a central question is not lost—namely, how, in this ongoing digital revolution that is seemingly remaking the world, can we still choose paths that make us more human, not less.

Used well, this technology can free up time for the relationships and activities that deserve our attention. It could also contribute to developments in a number of fields at the service of humanity, such as medicine, business, and education. There is also an opportunity for the Church in its engagement with those in the tech industry—not just to condemn what they’re building but to offer the wisdom many of them are asking for in how to build it responsibly.

The pope is not anti-technology, but he is clear about its challenges. Many of those challenges are similar to ones known to the Church before anyone had heard the term “artificial intelligence”: the cost to individuals, communities, and societies when relationships are sacrificed for productivity; human dignity made secondary to “progress”; and every human “limitation” seen simply as another obstacle just waiting to be transcended by the right technology. 

Brenden, in your many years of experience in evangelization and discipleship work, speaking to audiences and leading retreats and workshops all around the world, do you think that Pope Leo’s approach to this topic will resonate with Catholics worldwide? 

Pope Leo’s approach and insights can and are resonating with Catholics, not just because they do not require technical ability but because they go beyond technical questions to offer a robust and compelling vision that is uniquely Catholic. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

This past year, I have begun to offer workshops and input online and in-person, gauging the reception of this document and exploring wider engagement with AI in the Church. Catholics do not need to understand how a model is trained to feel the force of some of the pope’s central questions: What happens to human dignity when we start measuring ourselves against something we’ve built to imitate us, or let our formation as human beings be outsourced to it?

What I have also noticed when running sessions across quite different contexts is that the resonance tends to be strongest wherever people already feel the personal cost at work and at home. 

As Americans in an America-based apostolate, we can think in narrow terms of how encyclicals are received. Do you see that this will have a deep impact on how companies, legislative bodies, and the general populations respond to the AI path forward?

From my vantage point in Britain, it seems—to make a huge generalization—that business has been quick to explore the implementation of AI, governments have been slow to regulate or imagine policy implications, and the general public still sees it as somewhat of a novelty. In that context, one thing has struck me about the encyclical’s reception: the small signs of this document moving past the Church’s own audience. In the months since its release, there have been a few encouraging examples of major tech companies themselves raising questions similar to ones the pope raises, or others raising them with the major AI labs and governments. While it’s hard to neatly determine cause and effect in cultural influence and debates, it certainly seems that Magnifica Humanitas has arrived at the right moment. 

Time will tell how and whether it shapes wider attitudes and specific legislative approaches; history may be instructive here. When Leo XIV’s predecessor Leo XIII wrote Rerum Novarum in the late nineteenth century in the throes of the industrial revolution, it did not rewrite labor laws the week after it was published. It took decades for its moral logic to help form the Church’s social critique and contribute to how movements in society actually organized work. I’d expect something similar here. The immediate impact might not be a bill or act of parliament but perhaps a shift in what serious people inside and outside the Church feel able to say about the shape of the future AI is creating and the lives it touches.

What is a Word on Fire summit? How does it differ from other online offerings? What makes this summit unique, and what features of trusted experts and content-rich conversations can the participants expect? 

The word “summit” can conjure images of an elite gathering, but here we are using the word in the way a mountaineer might use it. Coming from the Latin summum, meaning the “highest point,” it indicates our intention to offer an intellectual and spiritual hike to a peak, as opposed to a walk in the park.

This is not a one-hour podcast, or our top ten quotations from the document with novel reflections (there are plenty of good resources online and in print already out there). Instead, we want to invite people into something that will require effort but will, we pray, reap a more profound reward: hard-won, shared wisdom. We think the effort involved appropriately honors the authority the document comes from, that of the Holy Father, as much as it reveres the profound themes it explores. 

One of the great benefits of this summit is the way this will be done alongside others. Most online formation happens in isolation. One of the real riches of the Word on Fire Institute as a whole, and in particular with this summit, is how we balance convenience and challenge. The content will be released daily for the six weeks of the program asynchronously, so people can engage on their own schedule and join from anywhere in the world. 

This summit also comes after Word on Fire’s own print release of the encyclical. We want to offer a rich environment of learning by bringing together thought-provoking posts alongside our rich repository of resources on the topic, including an Institute course on evangelization and AI, a previous Evangelization & Culture journal issue, numerous Evangelization & Culture Online articles, and previous live stream interviews.

Finally, what makes this summit distinctive is that we’re approaching it as evangelists, not just students. Alongside serious intellectual formation, we’ll be working through pastoral scenarios and giving people concrete challenges to put what they’re learning into practice. Each week is built around a different chapter of the encyclical. We will also have a live stream conversation with an expert from the field. Every week will close with a summary, so a member who has fallen behind can read one thing and know exactly what they’ve missed and how to catch up.

Artificial intelligence is relatively unlegislated and under-regulated. At the heart of evangelization is an encounter with Christ that radiates out, bringing Christ to the culture and proclaiming him in it. How would you encourage our rising generation of evangelists from every season of life to not fall under the influence of online personalities and so-called experts with a platform that may actually be contributing to the exploitative nature of AI for their readers/consumers? 

No technology or use of it is neutral. It takes on the character of whoever builds it, funds it, and uses it. Therefore, a first step in taking a more discerning approach with using such potent technology (whether it’s AI or social media) is simply to take time and ask some deeper questions about the content, the creators, and the platforms themselves. Before we unconsciously let someone else’s take on AI or other topics shape our thinking, we would benefit from reflecting on what it is they’re actually inviting us into and who benefits from our engagement.

But do we really need to take such a discerning and cautious approach? For the pope, I believe it boils down to a core concern that once we start measuring the human person against something we’ve built to surpass, enhance, or replace us, it becomes that bit easier to treat some human lives as less valuable, less useful, less worthy of dignity. That’s the real risk of formation-by-influencer: not that they might get a fact wrong here or there, but that they (or we) might be contributing to an ecosystem that quietly reshapes the vision of the human person.
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

One of the sharpest sections of Magnifica Humanitas deals directly with truth. In an age when almost anything can be manufactured or manipulated, the pope argues we need a renewed, critical education that lets us tell what’s true from what’s false. The loudest voices—or the ones with the highest production value—aren’t always worthy of the attention they receive. Volume and polish are not automatic markers of wisdom. To help in navigating the Wild West of the digital arena, we should seek to find oases that offer this kind of education and other people who want to exercise the spiritual muscles of discernment. I hope if you join us for the Magnifica Humanitas Summit, you will find such a space and such a community. 

None of this discernment happens automatically, and its success as an approach needs more than just education and a discerning attitude—it needs Christ. A Christ-centered life is the only foundation strong enough to withstand powerful ideologies and vested interests. Only the person who continues to put Christ at the center of their life is capable of finding the antidote to the fear and anxiety that is an all too common consequence of overexposure to the digital world. Closeness to Christ as a disciple is an ongoing education in the kind of freedom needed to test any claim, about AI or about themselves, against the way, the truth, and the life.

Thank you for taking the time to share about what this summit will entail and for your words of encouragement for our evangelists. How can folks register for this unique opportunity?

I am so excited for this summit, and I’d love to welcome anyone to be a part of it. Applications open now and close Friday, September 18. The summit runs for six weeks inside the Word on Fire Institute, and you can register here.

You don’t need to arrive with any expertise, just the willingness to stick with it for six weeks, and an open mind to let the pope’s wisdom take root.

items.title: WOF 542 | Why All Catholics Should Pray the Liturgy of the Hours
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

With so many forms of prayer already available, why should Catholics consider praying the Hours, and how can they practically get started?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Welcome back to the Word on Fire Show. I’m Matthew Petrusek, senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and the host of the Word on Fire Show. Thank you for joining us. The Liturgy of the Hours, or the “Divine Office,” is often associated exclusively with the spiritual practices of priests, monks, and nuns. To be sure, praying the Hours is an essential part of the lives of those who have formally taken religious vows. However, the prayer of the Church, as the Liturgy of the Hours is also called, is precisely that: a way of sanctifying the day for the whole Church, both laity and clergy alike. With so many forms of prayer already available, however, why should lay Catholics also consider praying the Hours? What, substantively, is distinctive about it? What are its origins? Moreover, given the size and complexity of the Hours—the full liturgy occupies four thick volumes of text with multiple ribbons to mark different sections—how, practically, can we get started? Here to explain the enduring theological and spiritual richness of the Liturgy of the Hours and how it deepens and enriches all Catholics’ lives, is Bishop Robert Barron.
